Vocab 0009 · Silmulator · from issue #18, commit 58b7e2d
71

ADC Reference Transfer Functions — Vocabulary

72

Eight terms behind the reference-aware ADC conversion. Each has a definition, a project example from the real code, a usage sentence, and a contrast with the term it's most often confused with.

73
74 75
76 reference voltage 77 full-scale code 78 transfer function 79 LSB voltage 80 ADC12VRSEL 81 REF_A 82 VeREF+ 83 ratiometric measurement 84
85 86 87
88

Reference voltage (VR+ / VR−)

89
the conversion's unit of measure
90
91
Definition
92
The voltage pair an ADC compares its input against: VR+ maps to the full-scale code, VR− maps to code 0. Every output code is a fraction of the span between them — the reference literally defines what one "unit" of the result means. Change the reference and the same physical input produces a different code.
93
Project example
94
In silmulator/devices/msp430.py, _adc_reference_voltage() resolves VR+ at conversion time — clock.vcc for AVCC, _veref_v for VEREF, or an ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V lookup for REF_A's outputs. VR− is fixed at AVSS (0 V) in this model. Before commit 58b7e2d, this function didn't exist and VR+ was a hardcoded 3.3.
95
Usage
96
"The RAW code looks huge because you left the 1.2-V reference voltage selected — 1.2 V in, 1.2 V reference, full scale out."
97
Contrast with: supply voltage
98
The supply (AVCC) powers the chip; the reference calibrates the measurement. They coincide only when AVCC is selected as the reference — and then supply drift becomes measurement drift, which is exactly what CPU:VCC 3.0 now lets a SIL test exercise.
99
100
101 102 103
104

Full-scale code (FS)

105
4095 · 1023 · 255
106
107
Definition
108
The maximum code an ADC can output: 2resolution − 1. It is produced when Vin ≥ VR+, so reading it means "at or above the reference" — possibly clipping — never a specific voltage.
109
Project example
110
msp430_faults.py computes max_code = (1 << resolution) - 1 and clamps with max(0, min(max_code, code)). The audit probe adc_ignores_reference asserts that 1.2 V against the 1.2-V VREF returns exactly 4095 — the input equals the reference, so the result is full scale.
111
Usage
112
"Inject 2.5 V against VREF2.0 and you'll read the full-scale code — the ideal 5118 clips to 4095."
113
Contrast with: full-scale voltage
114
The full-scale code is fixed by ADC:RESOLUTION (ADC12RES); the full-scale voltage is whatever reference is selected. Switching VREF2.5 → AVCC moves the voltage that produces 4095 from 2.5 V to 3.3 V, but 4095 itself never changes.
115
116
117 118 119
120

Transfer function

121
SLAU367P §34.2.1, Equation 13
122
123
Definition
124
The mapping from analog input to digital output code: NADC = FS × (Vin − VR−) / (VR+ − VR−), quantised and clamped. It makes explicit that an ADC code is a ratio of the reference span, not a voltage.
125
Project example
126
Implemented in FaultState.adc_code(): int(voltage / full_scale_v * max_code) with VR− = 0. Commit 58b7e2d's whole point was feeding the correct full_scale_v (the selected reference) into this function instead of the literal 3.3 — the CORNER profile then layers gain/offset/INL errors on top of the same ideal transfer curve.
127
Usage
128
"Work the transfer function forward to predict the code, and backward to recover volts — with the same reference both ways, or you get commit-58b7e2d's bug class."
129
Contrast with: calibration curve
130
The transfer function is the ideal, datasheet-defined mapping. A calibration curve characterises how a particular part deviates from it (gain, offset, INL — what the simulator's CORNER fault profile injects). You design against the transfer function; you correct against a calibration.
131
132
133 134 135
136

LSB voltage

137
(VR+ − VR−) / FS
138
139
Definition
140
The input-voltage width of one code step — the smallest voltage change the conversion can resolve. Set jointly by the reference span and the resolution: shrink the reference or raise the resolution, and each code is worth fewer microvolts.
141
Project example
142
With the references Silmulator now honours: 1.2 V / 4095 ≈ 293 µV per LSB under VREF, versus 3.3 V / 4095 ≈ 806 µV under default AVCC. The CORNER profile's INL spec is quoted in these units — a ±2.2-LSB bow in msp430_faults.py — which is only meaningful once you know the LSB's voltage value.
143
Usage
144
"Reading a 0–1 V sensor against AVCC wastes resolution — switch to VREF1.2 and your LSB voltage drops from 806 µV to 293 µV."
145
Contrast with: resolution (bit count)
146
Resolution is the number of steps (12-bit → 4096 of them); LSB voltage is how many volts each step spans. ADC:RESOLUTION changes the step count; ADC:REFERENCE changes the step size. Both knobs move the LSB voltage, only one moves the code range.
147
148
149 150 151
152

ADC12VRSEL

153
SLAU367P §34.2.4 — reference-select register field
154
155
Definition
156
The 4-bit field in the MSP430's ADC12MCTLx conversion-memory registers that selects which physical sources drive VR+ and VR−. Because it is a register field, the set of possible references is finite and fixed by silicon — there is no encoding for an arbitrary voltage.
157
Project example
158
VALID_ADC_REFERENCES = frozenset({"AVCC", "VEREF"} | set(ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V)) in msp430.py mirrors the VRSEL choices the model exposes. ADC:REFERENCE BANANA — or 1.8 — has no encoding, so _adc_ref raises ScpiError(-224, "Illegal ADC reference: …"), matching test_reference_out_of_range_rejected.
159
Usage
160
"The SCPI layer rejects free-form references because ADC12VRSEL is an enum in silicon, not a dial."
161
Contrast with: REFVSEL
162
ADC12VRSEL (in the ADC) picks which source feeds the reference inputs; REFVSEL (in REF_A, §33.3.1) picks which voltage — 1.2/2.0/2.5 V — the internal reference module generates. Silmulator folds both into one token: VREF2.5 effectively sets REFVSEL = 10b and points VRSEL at the internal reference.
163
164
165 166 167
168

REF_A

169
SLAU367P §33 — shared reference module
170
171
Definition
172
The FR5994's on-chip reference generator: a bandgap-derived module shared by the ADC and comparators that outputs a precise, supply-independent 1.2, 2.0, or 2.5 V (selected by REFVSEL, reset default 00b = 1.2 V).
173
Project example
174
Modelled by the ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V dict — {"VREF": 1.2, "VREF1.2": 1.2, "VREF2.0": 2.0, "VREF2.5": 2.5} — with bare VREF deliberately mapped to the REFVSEL reset value. The audit's MISSING list notes what is still absent: REFCTL0 semantics (REFON/REFOUT/REFGENRDY/REFBGRDY bits and the request/ready handshake).
175
Usage
176
"For an absolute battery-voltage reading, don't reference AVCC — take REF_A's 2.5-V output so supply sag can't skew the measurement."
177
Contrast with: AVCC as a reference
178
REF_A's outputs are fixed absolute voltages, immune to supply drift; AVCC tracks the supply (Silmulator reads clock.vcc live). Absolute measurements want REF_A; ratiometric sensors powered from the rail want AVCC.
179
180
181 182 183
184

VeREF+

185
SLASE54D Table 7-1 — external reference pin
186
187
Definition
188
The MSP430 pin through which a board supplies its own external positive reference — typically a precision reference IC (2.048 V, 4.096 V, …). Its voltage is a board-design decision, not a chip property, and it has no defined reset state after BOR.
189
Project example
190
Commit 58b7e2d added self._veref_v (default 1.2, restored by *RST) and the two-parameter SCPI form ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.1 — select the pin and declare what the board wires to it. A non-numeric voltage raises ScpiError(-104, …), pinned by test_veref_voltage_param_must_be_numeric.
191
Usage
192
"Our flight board has a 2.048-V reference IC on VeREF+, so the SIL setup sends ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.048 before any conversion."
193
Contrast with: VREF (internal)
194
VREF tokens select REF_A's on-chip outputs — fixed at 1.2/2.0/2.5 V, no configuration needed. VeREF+ is off-chip: any voltage the board provides, which is why it is the only reference whose value the test must declare (and the only one with a -104 failure mode).
195
196
197 198 199
200

Ratiometric measurement

201
when the supply cancels out
202
203
Definition
204
A measurement arrangement where the sensor's output and the ADC's reference derive from the same source, so the conversion measures the sensor's fraction and the source's absolute value cancels out of the transfer function: N = FS × (k·AVCC)/AVCC = FS × k.
205
Project example
206
Selecting ADC:REFERENCE AVCC makes _adc_reference_voltage() return self.clock.vcc live. A divider-style sensor modelled by injecting k × vcc reads the same code before and after CPU:VCC 3.0 — while an absolute injection like the fixed 1.2 V shifts from 1489 to 1638, which is how a SIL test tells the two arrangements apart.
207
Usage
208
"The potentiometer is powered from the rail, so keep the conversion ratiometric — referencing it to VREF2.5 would re-introduce the supply drift you're trying to cancel."
209
Contrast with: absolute measurement
210
Absolute measurement answers "how many volts?" and needs a supply-independent reference (REF_A or VeREF+). Ratiometric measurement answers "what fraction of the excitation?" and wants the supply as the reference. Choosing the wrong mode for the sensor type is a real firmware bug class the reference-aware model can now surface.
211

4	
5	| Term | Definition |
6	|------|------------|
7	| ConnectionPort | A `QGraphicsEllipseItem` child of a block that holds `port_id`, `parent_block`, and `connected_to` (the peer port, or None). Coloured blue when free, green when connected. |

10	| hardware_docs/ | The folder in the repo where vendor PDFs, SCPI command tables, and notes are stored. Not auto-parsed; feeds the custom-block authoring workflow. |
11	| custom block spec | A JSON file in `silmulator/custom_blocks/` that declares a block's name, colour, port layout, and SCPI command map. Loaded at startup by `discover_specs()`. |
12	| SIL | Software-in-the-Loop: both the controller logic and the instruments are simulated in software. No real hardware. |
13	| HIL | Hardware-in-the-Loop: the real embedded controller runs in real time; only the instruments/plant are simulated. |
14	| CIL | Code-in-the-Loop: actual source files are the artifact under test; SCPI calls extracted from them are replayed against simulated instruments. The Code Input block enables this. |
15	| SCPI | Standard Commands for Programmable Instruments (IEEE 488.2). A tree-structured text command language used by lab instruments and simulated here. |
16	| reference voltage | The voltage pair (VR+/VR−) an ADC compares its input against — the conversion's unit of measure. In the MSP430 model, `_adc_reference_voltage()` resolves VR+ from the selected `ADC:REFERENCE` (AVCC live via `clock.vcc`, REF_A outputs, or VeREF+); VR− is fixed at AVSS (0 V). |
17	| full-scale code | The maximum ADC output, 2^resolution − 1 (4095/1023/255). Produced when Vin ≥ VR+, so it means "at or above the reference" — possibly clipping — never a specific voltage. Clamped in `FaultState.adc_code()`. |
18	| transfer function | The input→code mapping NADC = FS × (Vin − VR−)/(VR+ − VR−) (SLAU367P §34.2.1 Eq. 13). An ADC code is a ratio of the reference span, not a voltage. Implemented as `int(voltage / full_scale_v * max_code)`, clamped. |
19	| LSB voltage | The input-voltage width of one code step: (VR+ − VR−)/FS. ≈293 µV under the 1.2-V VREF vs ≈806 µV under 3.3-V AVCC at 12 bits — the reference sets granularity as well as range. |
20	| ADC12VRSEL | The 4-bit ADC12MCTLx field (SLAU367P §34.2.4) selecting which physical sources drive VR+/VR−. A finite register encoding — mirrored by `VALID_ADC_REFERENCES`, which is why `ADC:REFERENCE BANANA` is rejected with SCPI -224. |
21	| REF_A | The FR5994's shared internal reference module (SLAU367P §33): bandgap-derived 1.2/2.0/2.5-V outputs selected by REFVSEL (reset default 00b = 1.2 V). Modelled by the `ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V` dict; bare `VREF` maps to the reset default. |
22	| VeREF+ | The external positive-reference pin (SLASE54D Table 7-1) — board-supplied, no defined reset state. Modelled as `_veref_v`, set via `ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,<v>` (non-numeric voltage → SCPI -104), reset to 1.2 by `*RST`. |
23	| ratiometric measurement | Referencing the ADC to the same source that powers the sensor so the supply cancels: N = FS × (k·AVCC)/AVCC = FS × k. The reason AVCC exists as a reference choice; testable because AVCC reads `clock.vcc` live at conversion time. |
24	| register width | The number of physical flip-flops in a register, fixing its representable values at 0 … 2^width − 1. TAxR/TAxCCRn are 16-bit; writes outside 0–0xFFFF are rejected with SCPI -222 (`_timer_count`, `_timer_cc_val`). Python ints are unbounded, so the model must enforce width explicitly. |
25	| encoding | The finite mapping from a register field's bit patterns to behaviours — an n-bit field reaches at most 2^n values. The timer divider is ID (2 bits) × TAIDEX (3 bits), max /64; /128 has no encoding and draws -224. Width bounds magnitude; encoding bounds meaning. |
26	| reachable state space | The set of states real hardware can occupy — the closure of all field encodings. A simulator's accepted inputs must stay inside it: accepting an unreachable state (the old /128) silently voids every downstream SIL result. The accepted set may be a documented *subset* (the power-of-two dividers). |
27	| write masking | Truncating an over-width write to the register width (`value & 0xFFFF`) instead of refusing it — what a 16-bit bus does physically. Silmulator rejects with -222 instead; `test_count_over_16bit_rejected_or_masked` blesses either policy, forbidding only verbatim storage. |
28	| TAIDEX | The 3-bit input divider expansion field in TAxEX0 (÷1…8), cascaded after ID (÷1/2/4/8) in TAxCTL. Effective divider = ID × TAIDEX product: 20 reachable values, max 8×8 = /64 — why `TIMERA0:CLOCK:DIVIDER 128` is impossible and rejected. |
29	| CAP bit | The per-CC-unit mode bit in TAxCCTLn: compare (CCRn holds a written value) vs capture (an edge latches the count into CCRn). Stored state since a20fbb1 (`cc_mode` dict, -224 validation); capture *events* are out of scope — time does not pass. |
30	| register aliasing | Two interface names denoting one physical register, modeled as delegation to a single store. PERIOD IS TAxCCR0 (SLAU367P §25.2.3.1): `_timer_period` is `return self._timer_cc_val(cmd, ts, 0)` — the old independent `period` field was the double-store bug class. |
31	| stored-state modeling | Simulating a device as a validated state machine with no autonomous dynamics: registers hold what was written; counting, latching, and interrupts never happen because time does not pass. Model configuration fully, document dynamics as out of scope — never fake them. |

Lesson 0013 · Silmulator · from issue #22, commit 07f1f69

MSP430X: 20-bit Registers on a 16-bit-looking ISA

Why this matters: the FR5994 carries 256 KB of FRAM, but a 16-bit pointer can only see 64 KB. Until commit 07f1f69 the model truncated every 20-bit register value to 16 bits, accepted impossible program counters, and reset to a constant borrowed from a different chip — three silent lies to every SIL test.

Sections:
☐ 1. One ISA, two widths
☐ 2. Binary compatibility
☐ 3. The mask fix (07f1f69)
☐ 4. PC validation
☐ 5. Reset is a fetch
☐ 6. Reset across families
☐ 7. Why SIL cares
☐ 8. Misconceptions
☐ 9. Quiz
☐ 10. Scenarios

1. One ISA, Two Register Widths

The original MSP430 CPU is a textbook 16-bit machine: sixteen 16-bit registers (R0–R15), a 16-bit ALU, and a 16-bit address bus — a 64-KB world. Then TI started shipping parts whose memory outgrew the address bus. The FR5994 has 256 KB of FRAM; you cannot point at 256 KB with 16 bits.

TI's answer was the MSP430X CPU (CPUX): keep the instruction set looking 16-bit, but widen every register to 20 bits and the address space to 1 MB (220 = 1,048,576 addresses, 0x00000–0xFFFFF). SLAU367P §4.3 is blunt about it: R0–R15 are physically 20 bits of flip-flops, even when 16-bit code is running.

MSP430 CPUMSP430X CPU (CPUX — what the FR5994 has)
Register width R0–R1516 bits20 bits (max value 0xFFFFF = 1,048,575)
Address space64 KB (0x0000–0xFFFF)1 MB (0x00000–0xFFFFF)
PC / SP16-bit, even20-bit, bit 0 still always 0
Old 16-bit binaries—Run unchanged (binary compatible)

Where the FR5994 keeps its bytes (SLASE54D memory map)

RegionAddress rangeSize16-bit reachable?
RAM0x1C00–0x3BFF8 KByes
FRAM (code start)0x4000–0xFF7F≈48 KByes
Interrupt vectors0xFF80–0xFFFF (reset at 0xFFFE)128 Byes
Extended FRAM0x10000–0x43FFF208 KBno — needs 20 bits

Do the arithmetic once and the whole issue clicks: 48 KB + 208 KB = 256 KB, and 81% of the FR5994's FRAM lives above 0xFFFF. Every pointer into that region — every lookup table, every logging buffer parked in upper FRAM — is a value that a 16-bit register model physically cannot hold.

💡 The mental model
Think of CPUX as a 16-bit machine wearing 20-bit gloves. The instruction encodings, the word size, the even-address rule — all inherited from the 16-bit parent. But the registers underneath have four extra bits (bits 19:16), which carve the 1-MB space into sixteen 64-KB pages. A simulator that masks with 0xFFFF is amputating exactly those four bits.

2. Binary Compatibility: the Upper-4-Bits Contract

How do you widen every register without breaking twenty years of compiled 16-bit code? SLAU367P §4.3 defines a strict contract for how the two widths coexist in one register file:

  • 16-bit (word, .W) writes clear bits 19:16. MOV.W #0x2345, R4 leaves R4 = 0x02345 — never a stale upper nibble. Old code that "thinks" R4 is 16-bit sees exactly 16-bit behaviour.
  • 16-bit reads return the low word. The upper 4 bits are invisible to non-extended instructions.
  • Extended instructions (MOVA, CALLA, BRA, the .A address-word forms) use all 20 bits. New code opts into the wide world explicitly.

The result is binary compatibility: an unmodified MSP430 binary produces bit-identical register states on a CPUX part, because it can neither set nor observe bits 19:16. The 4 extra bits are only reachable through instructions the old ISA doesn't contain.

20-bit register  =  [19:16] page bits  |  [15:0] classic 16-bit word bits 19:16 select one of sixteen 64-KB pages; a .W write zeroes them, a .A write sets them
⚠ Where the simulator sits
Silmulator's SCPI surface (CPU:REGISTER n,value) doesn't distinguish .W from .A writes — every write behaves like a full-width store masked to the register's physical 20 bits. What the model must never do is pretend the flip-flops above bit 15 don't exist. That was exactly the pre-07f1f69 bug.

3. The Mask Fix — What Commit 07f1f69 Changed in _cpu_reg

The compliance audit (docs/audits/msp430-compliance-report.md) flagged CPU:REGISTER as NON_COMPLIANT: "CPUX registers R0–R15 are 20-bit; writes are masked to 16 bits (0xFFFF), silently truncating any 20-bit value." One hex digit in a mask:

# silmulator/silmulator/devices/msp430.py — _cpu_reg()
# BEFORE 07f1f69:
self._registers[reg] = int(cmd.params[1], 0) & 0xFFFF    # 16 bits — wrong CPU
# AFTER 07f1f69:
self._registers[reg] = int(cmd.params[1], 0) & 0xFFFFF   # 20 bits — CPUX (SLAU367P §4.3)

Worked example 1 — the audit probe's exact value: 0x12345

0x12345 = 0001 0010 0011 0100 0101₂  (bit 16 set — a pointer into the second 64-KB page)

old:  0x12345 & 0xFFFF  = 0x2345   # bits 19:16 amputated: 74,565 → 9,029
new:  0x12345 & 0xFFFFF = 0x12345  # round-trips intact

The probe in scripts/audit_msp430.py was renamed from probe_cpu_reg_16bit to probe_cpu_reg_20bit and now asserts the compliant behaviour:

def probe_cpu_reg_20bit(dev: MSP430) -> bool:
    """CPUX registers are 20-bit; the model masks writes to 20 bits (0xFFFFF)."""
    dev.process("CPU:REGISTER 4,0x12345")
    return dev.process("CPU:REGISTER? 4") == "0x12345"

Worked example 2 — 0xFFFFF round-trips

CPU:REGISTER 7,0xFFFFF        # the largest 20-bit value, 1,048,575
  store: 0xFFFFF & 0xFFFFF = 0xFFFFF
CPU:REGISTER? 7  →  "0xFFFFF"
  # before the fix: 0xFFFFF & 0xFFFF = 0xFFFF (65,535) — the top of page 0,
  # a completely different address, with no error queued

Why the query still prints correctly

The read path is return f"0x{self._registers[reg]:04X}". The 04X is a minimum width, not a truncation: 0x2345 prints as 0x2345, and 0xFFFFF grows naturally to five digits, 0xFFFFF. No format change was needed — only the mask.

Masking is the right policy here (and rejection isn't)

Recall the write masking idea from lesson 0010: a register with N flip-flops physically cannot store more than N bits — hardware "masks" by construction. Modelling R4 as value & 0xFFFFF mirrors the silicon. The bug wasn't that the model masked; it's that it masked to the wrong CPU's width, turning legal FR5994 values into different legal values with no error. That is the worst failure mode a simulator has: not wrong loudly, wrong plausibly.

4. The PC Gets Validation, Not Masking

The program counter (R0) has an extra architectural rule the other registers don't: bit 0 is always 0 (SLAU367P §4.3.1). Instructions are word-aligned; an odd PC cannot exist in silicon. Before the commit, CPU:PC accepted anything — odd values, 24-bit values — and the audit scored it ACCEPTS_INVALID. The fix adds two checks:

def _cpu_pc(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
    """Program counter (SLAU367P §4.3.1): 20-bit, bit 0 always 0 (word-aligned)."""
    if cmd.is_query:
        return f"0x{self._pc:04X}"
    if cmd.params:
        v = int(cmd.params[0], 0)
        if not 0 <= v <= 0xFFFFF:
            raise ScpiError(-222, "PC out of range (0-0xFFFFF)")
        if v & 1:
            raise ScpiError(-222, "PC must be word-aligned (bit 0 is always 0)")
        self._pc = v
    return ""

Worked example — three writes, three outcomes

CPU:PC 0x4001    →  -222 "PC must be word-aligned (bit 0 is always 0)"
                    # 0x4001 & 1 = 1 — odd, impossible in hardware; PC unchanged

CPU:PC 0x123457  →  -222 "PC out of range (0-0xFFFFF)"
                    # 1,193,047 > 1,048,575: the RANGE check fires first —
                    # the value is also odd, but the alignment check never runs

CPU:PC 0xFFFFE   →  accepted
                    # 1,048,574: even, ≤ 0xFFFFF — the highest legal PC

The audit probe probe_cpu_pc_validated checks both directions: CPU:PC 0x123457 must queue exactly one error and leave dev._pc untouched, and a subsequent CPU:PC 0x4000 must be accepted without adding a second error.

Why reject here, but mask in _cpu_reg?

Two different hardware truths, two policies. An over-wide write to a data register maps onto something silicon actually does (only 20 flip-flops latch — write masking). An odd PC maps onto nothing: no instruction sequence, no bus cycle, no debugger poke can produce it, because bit 0 of R0 is hardwired to 0. Values with no reachable hardware state get rejected loudly with -222 "Data out of range" — the same policy lesson 0010 established for over-width timer registers.

5. Reset Is a Fetch, Not a Jump to a Constant

The old model did this on CPU:RESET: self._pc = 0xC000. Real MSP430 hardware does something categorically different at the end of every BOR/POR/PUC reset chain (SLAU367P §1.2): it performs a memory read. The word at address 0xFFFE — the reset vector, placed there by the linker as part of the program image — is loaded into the PC. Reset behaviour is a property of the firmware, not the silicon.

# msp430.py — added by 07f1f69
def _reset_vector_pc(self) -> int:
    """PC on reset (SLAU367P §4.3, §1.2): fetched from the reset vector at
    0xFFFE/0xFFFF (little-endian word). Defaults to 0x4000 — FRAM code
    start (SLASE54D memory map) — when the vector has not been written.
    """
    lo = self._memory.get(0xFFFE)
    hi = self._memory.get(0xFFFF)
    if lo is None and hi is None:
        return 0x4000
    return ((hi or 0) << 8) | (lo or 0)

Both _cpu_reset and the device-wide *RST path now call this instead of assigning a constant.

Worked example — the little-endian word read

MEMORY:WRITE 0xFFFE,0x00      # LOW byte at the LOWER address (little-endian)
MEMORY:WRITE 0xFFFF,0xC0      # HIGH byte at the higher address
CPU:RESET
CPU:PC?  →  0xC000            # (0xC0 << 8) | 0x00 = 49,152 = 0xC000

This is exactly what probe_cpu_reset_vector_pc exercises: first CPU:RESET with the vector unwritten (expects the 0x4000 default), then the two byte writes above and a second reset (expects 0xC000).

Why 0x4000 as the default — and why 0xC000 was wrong

When nothing has been loaded at 0xFFFE/0xFFFF, the model needs some sane PC. The commit picks 0x4000, the FR5994's FRAM code start (SLASE54D memory map) — where a linker places the first byte of code on this part. The old constant 0xC000 is not FR5994-specific at all; it's the flash start of older, smaller MSP430s (a 16-KB flash part maps 0xC000–0xFFFF). The audit's words: "0xC000 is not FR5994-specific (code FRAM starts at 0x4000)." A constant copied from the wrong chip is a compliance bug even when the mechanism looks harmless.

Two subtleties worth pinning

  • The default only applies when BOTH bytes are unwritten. The guard is if lo is None and hi is None. Write only 0xFFFE,0x34 and reset gives PC = (0 << 8) | 0x34 = 0x0034 — a half-written vector is honoured as-is, not "fixed up" to the default.
  • The vector is a 16-bit word, so reset always lands below 0x10000. (hi << 8) | lo can never exceed 0xFFFF. That matches hardware: MSP430X interrupt/reset vectors stay 16-bit, so the reset entry point must live in the lower 64 KB — code in extended FRAM (0x10000+) is reached only after startup, via CALLA/BRA with full 20-bit targets.
📌 A ripple into the WDT probe
probe_wdt_stub used to assert dev._pc == 0xC000 ("a wrong WDT password did not cause a reset"). With the constant gone, the commit rewrites it to capture pc_before = dev._pc and compare against that — the probe's real claim was always "PC unchanged", and hardcoding the reset constant into it was a hidden coupling the fix flushed out.

6. How Other MCU Families Come Out of Reset

The MSP430 is a von Neumann machine: one flat address space holds RAM, FRAM, peripherals, and the vector table. That's why MEMORY:WRITE 0xFFFE,… can set the reset target — the vector is just bytes at an address, readable and writable like any other. Different families answer "where does execution start?" in two fundamentally different ways:

FamilyReset mechanismWhat lives at the reset location
MSP430Hardware fetches the word at 0xFFFE into PC (little-endian)A pointer (data)
6502Hardware fetches the word at 0xFFFC/0xFFFD into PC (little-endian)A pointer — the closest cousin to MSP430's flow
ARM Cortex-MHardware fetches two words: initial SP from 0x00000000, reset-handler address from 0x00000004 (bit 0 set = Thumb)Two pointers
AVRExecution simply begins at flash address 0x0000An instruction (usually JMP main_init)
8051Execution begins at 0x0000An instruction
x86Execution begins at physical 0xFFFFFFF0An instruction (a far jump into firmware)

Two camps: pointer-fetch families (MSP430, 6502, Cortex-M) where reset performs a memory read and the vector's content is an address, versus execute-at-fixed-address families (AVR, 8051, x86) where reset performs a jump and the vector location holds code. Details that separate even the cousins:

  • MSP430 and 6502 both put the vector at the top of a 64-KB map and read it little-endian; Cortex-M puts its table at the bottom.
  • Cortex-M initialises SP in hardware (from offset 0x0). MSP430 hardware loads only the PC — the startup code must set up the stack itself.
  • Bit 0 semantics invert: a Cortex-M reset-handler address has bit 0 set (the Thumb bit); an MSP430 PC has bit 0 always clear. Port a test harness between them without knowing this and every PC assertion breaks.
  • AVR is a Harvard machine — its "vector" lives in a separate program space that data reads can't even address, so an AVR simulator could not model reset with a plain memory dict the way _reset_vector_pc() does. The MSP430's von Neumann layout is what makes the Silmulator implementation this small.

7. Why This Matters for SIL Testing

All three fixes share one theme: the model was silently blessing states the FR5994 cannot reach, and silently destroying states it can.

The truncation bug class

Firmware for a 256-KB part keeps big data in extended FRAM. A SIL script that seeds a pointer register — CPU:REGISTER 9,0x28000, say, a table in upper FRAM — used to get 0x8000 stored instead (0x28000 & 0xFFFF), with no error. Every downstream check then ran against an address in the wrong 64-KB page. Worse, if the test's own expectations were written from the same 16-bit habit, sim and test agreed with each other and the suite passed — the "wrong in the same direction" trap from lesson 0009, now in the address domain.

What the reset-vector fetch unlocks

  • Startup-flow tests: a test can load a firmware image's actual vector (MEMORY:WRITE 0xFFFE,lo / 0xFFFF,hi) and assert that reset lands on the image's entry point — the linker's work is now observable in simulation.
  • Reset-source coverage: both CPU:RESET and *RST route through _reset_vector_pc(), so device-level and CPU-level resets behave consistently.
  • Invalid-PC injection: scripts that used to "test" recovery from PC = 0x123457 were testing a fiction; the model now refuses to enter states hardware can't express, with -222.

The scoreboard

The compliance report moved 34.3% → 38.2% (35 → 39 of 102 scored families): CPU:PC, CPU:REGISTER, CPU:REG, and CPU:RESET all flipped to COMPLIANT. The same commit also legalised POWER:MODE LPM3.5 (a documented FR5994 mode the model used to reject) — though POWER:MODE stays PARTIAL because low-power modes still don't gate the clocks. And the strict-xfail ledger worked as designed: test_lpm35_accepted dropped its @pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True) marker and became a plain regression guard.

8. Often Confused

ConfusionThe distinction
"The MSP430 is 16-bit, so registers max out at 0xFFFF" The ISA heritage and word size are 16-bit; on CPUX parts the register file is physically 20-bit (SLAU367P §4.3). 0xFFFFF is a perfectly legal register value on an FR5994 — a model that can't hold it is modelling the wrong CPU.
Masking vs. validating a write Masking (& 0xFFFFF) mirrors physical register width — what flip-flops do. Validation (-222) rejects states with no hardware existence — an odd PC. Commit 07f1f69 deliberately uses both, one per situation.
"Reset jumps to a fixed address" On MSP430, reset is a memory fetch: PC ← word at 0xFFFE. The landing address is part of the firmware image (the linker writes it), not a property of the chip. The old self._pc = 0xC000 encoded the misconception literally.
"The reset vector holds an instruction" Family-specific. MSP430/6502/Cortex-M vectors hold addresses (data); AVR/8051/x86 reset locations hold code. Confusing the camps breaks ported test harnesses.
"A 20-bit PC means a 20-bit reset vector" MSP430X vectors stayed 16-bit words. (hi << 8) | lo ≤ 0xFFFF always — reset lands in the lower 64 KB, and extended FRAM is reached later via CALLA/BRA.
"0x{v:04X} truncates to 4 hex digits" 04X is a minimum field width with zero-padding. 0x2345 prints 4 digits; 0xFFFFF prints all 5. The read path needed no change for 20-bit values.
-222 on PC writes vs. -222 on register number Same SCPI code, two different range checks in _cpu_reg/_cpu_pc: register index outside 0–15, and PC value outside the even 20-bit space. Read the message text, not just the number.

9. Quiz

Q1. After commit 07f1f69, a test sends CPU:REGISTER 7,0xFFFFF and then CPU:REGISTER? 7. What comes back?

  • 0xFFFFF

Q2. A script sends CPU:PC 0x123457. Which error is queued?

  • -222 "PC must be word-aligned (bit 0 is always 0)"
  • No error — the value is stored as-is
  • No error — the value is masked to 0x23457

Q3. A test runs MEMORY:WRITE 0xFFFE,0x00, then MEMORY:WRITE 0xFFFF,0xC0, then CPU:RESET. What is the PC?

  • 0xC000 — (hi << 8) | lo with lo = 0x00, hi = 0xC0
  • 0x00C0
  • 0x4000 — the default always applies after CPU:RESET
  • 0xC000 — because reset always forces the constant 0xC000

Q4. Why does _reset_vector_pc() default to 0x4000 rather than keeping 0xC000?

  • 0x4000 is the FR5994's FRAM code start (SLASE54D); 0xC000 belongs to a different part's memory map
  • 0x4000 is word-aligned and 0xC000 is not
  • 0x4000 is where the reset vector itself is stored

10. Scenarios — Check Your Understanding

Scenario A: Firmware keeps a calibration table at 0x28000 in extended FRAM. A pre-07f1f69 SIL script seeded the pointer with CPU:REGISTER 9,0x28000, read it back, and its assertions passed anyway. Reconstruct what actually happened, and what the same script does today.
Show answer 
old:  0x28000 & 0xFFFF  = 0x8000     ← bits 19:16 (0x2) silently dropped
      CPU:REGISTER? 9  → "0x8000"    ← a valid-looking address in the WRONG page
new:  0x28000 & 0xFFFFF = 0x28000    ← round-trips intact

The old model stored 0x8000 — page 0 instead of page 2 — with no error queued. If the test's expected value was written by someone with the same 16-bit habit (or computed from the truncated read-back itself), simulator and test agreed with each other and everything passed. That's the cancelling-errors trap: the model wasn't wrong loudly, it was wrong plausibly. Today the value round-trips, so an assertion against 0x8000 would now fail — correctly exposing that the test had encoded the truncation. This is why the audit probe (probe_cpu_reg_20bit) asserts the full "0x12345" string rather than anything derived from the model's own output.

Scenario B: A teammate writes MEMORY:WRITE 0xFFFE,0xC0, resets, and expects PC = 0xC000 — but CPU:PC? returns 0x00C0. They claim the reset-vector code is broken. Diagnose it.
Show answer

Endianness. The MSP430 is little-endian: 0xFFFE holds the LOW byte of the vector, 0xFFFF holds the high byte. They wrote 0xC0 into the low byte and nothing into the high byte, so _reset_vector_pc() computes ((None or 0) << 8) | 0xC0 = 0x00C0 = 192.

Two extra teaching points hide here. First, the 0x4000 default did not apply — the guard is if lo is None and hi is None, and lo exists, so the half-written vector is honoured as-is rather than "fixed up". Second, the result 0x00C0 is even and in range, so nothing downstream rejects it — garbage in the vector produces a faithful garbage jump, exactly like hardware. The fix: MEMORY:WRITE 0xFFFE,0x00 and MEMORY:WRITE 0xFFFF,0xC0.

Scenario C: You're porting a startup-flow test from an STM32 (Cortex-M) harness. It writes the entry-point address at vector offset 0x4, expects the address to have bit 0 set, and asserts the stack pointer was loaded by hardware. List everything that breaks against the MSP430 model and why.
Show answer

Nearly everything — the two families are both "pointer-fetch" architectures, but every detail differs:

  • Vector location: Cortex-M reads the reset handler from 0x00000004 (table at the bottom of memory); MSP430 reads it from 0xFFFE (top of the 64-KB map). Writing to offset 0x4 configures nothing on the MSP430.
  • Bit 0 semantics invert: a Cortex-M vector must have bit 0 set (Thumb bit); on MSP430, PC bit 0 is always 0, and CPU:PC rejects odd values with -222 "PC must be word-aligned". The harness's odd entry address is an impossible MSP430 state.
  • SP is not hardware-loaded: Cortex-M fetches the initial SP from offset 0x0; MSP430 hardware loads only the PC from the vector — startup code initialises the stack. The SP assertion has no MSP430 counterpart (and _cpu_reset zeroes all of R0–R15's stored values, including R1/SP).
  • Vector width: Cortex-M vectors are 32-bit words; MSP430 reset vectors are 16-bit — the expected entry point must be below 0x10000.

The portable core of the test is only the idea: "reset fetches the entry point from the image, so load a vector and assert PC lands there" — which on this model is the MEMORY:WRITE 0xFFFE/0xFFFF + CPU:RESET + CPU:PC? sequence from probe_cpu_reset_vector_pc.

Vocab 0013 · Silmulator · from issue #22, commit 07f1f69

MSP430X 20-bit Registers — Vocabulary

Eight terms behind the 20-bit CPUX fix. Each has a definition, a project example from the real code, a usage sentence, and a contrast with the term it's most often confused with.

MSP430X / CPUX 20-bit register address space word alignment reset vector PUC-time PC fetch write masking width binary compatibility

MSP430X / CPUX

SLAU367P §4 — the extended CPU in the FR5994
Definition
TI's extension of the 16-bit MSP430 CPU: registers R0–R15 widened to 20 bits and the address space to 1 MB, while keeping every 16-bit instruction encoding working unchanged. New extended instructions (MOVA, CALLA, BRA, the .A forms) carry full 20-bit operands; everything else behaves exactly like the original CPU.
Project example
Commit 07f1f69's _cpu_reg docstring pins it: "R0-R15 (SLAU367P §4.3): CPUX registers are 20-bit, masked accordingly" — and the store became int(cmd.params[1], 0) & 0xFFFFF. The audit's old finding ("writes are masked to 16 bits, silently truncating any 20-bit value") described a model of the wrong CPU.
Usage
"The FR5994 is a CPUX part — if your simulator can't hold 0x12345 in R4, it's simulating a chip TI stopped designing years ago."
Contrast with: the original MSP430 CPU
The original CPU has 16-bit registers and a 64-KB world; CPUX has 20-bit registers and 1 MB. Same instruction set at the 16-bit level — the difference only shows when values or addresses cross 0xFFFF, which on a 256-KB-FRAM part happens constantly.

20-bit register

max value 0xFFFFF = 1,048,575
Definition
A register built from 20 physical flip-flops, representing 0…220−1. On CPUX, all of R0–R15 are 20-bit (SLAU367P §4.3); bits 19:16 act as page-select bits over sixteen 64-KB pages. Sixteen-bit (.W) writes clear those upper 4 bits; extended instructions read and write all 20.
Project example
The one-digit fix in msp430.py: self._registers[reg] = int(cmd.params[1], 0) & 0xFFFFF (was & 0xFFFF). probe_cpu_reg_20bit verifies it: write 0x12345 to R4, read back the string "0x12345" — under the old mask it came back "0x2345".
Usage
"That pointer register holds a 20-bit value — mask it with 0xFFFF anywhere in the pipeline and you've quietly moved it into the wrong 64-KB page."
Contrast with: register width (lesson 0010)
"Register width" is the general concept — the flip-flop count that bounds representable values. "20-bit register" is that concept instantiated for CPUX. The timer lesson's registers are genuinely 16-bit and must stay so; the CPU's are 20-bit and must not be modelled narrower. Same principle, opposite failure directions.

Address space

0x00000–0xFFFFF — 1 MB on CPUX
Definition
The set of addresses a CPU can generate: 2N locations for N address bits. CPUX has N = 20 → 1,048,576 addresses. On the von Neumann MSP430, one flat space holds RAM, FRAM, peripherals, and the vector table — there is no separate "program memory".
Project example
The FR5994 map (SLASE54D) that the fix serves: RAM 0x1C00–0x3BFF, code FRAM from 0x4000 (the reset default in _reset_vector_pc()), vectors 0xFF80–0xFFFF, and 208 of the 256 KB of FRAM in the extended region 0x10000–0x43FFF — reachable only with 20-bit values, which is why CPU:PC now validates 0 <= v <= 0xFFFFF.
Usage
"Eighty-one percent of this part's FRAM sits above the 64-KB line — the address space is the whole reason CPUX exists."
Contrast with: memory actually populated
The address space is what the CPU can point at; the memory map is what actually answers. The FR5994 populates well under half of its 1-MB space — a legal PC like 0xFFFFE may still point at nothing. Silmulator's _memory dict mirrors this: any address can be written, unwritten ones read back as 0.

Word alignment

even addresses only — PC bit 0 ≡ 0
Definition
The rule that multi-byte accesses start at addresses divisible by the access size: MSP430 words (2 bytes) live at even addresses. For the PC it is architectural, not conventional — SLAU367P §4.3.1 says bit 0 of the PC is always 0, so an odd PC has no silicon state at all.
Project example
_cpu_pc() after 07f1f69: if v & 1: raise ScpiError(-222, "PC must be word-aligned (bit 0 is always 0)"). CPU:PC 0x4001 queues -222 and leaves the PC untouched; CPU:PC 0xFFFFE — the highest legal PC — is accepted.
Usage
"The test injected an odd PC to 'simulate corruption' — but hardware can't even represent that state, so the model rightly refuses it with -222."
Contrast with: byte addressability
Memory itself is byte-addressable — MEMORY:WRITE 0xFFFF,0xC0 (an odd address) is perfectly fine for a byte. Alignment constrains word accesses and the PC specifically. Odd address ≠ illegal address; odd program counter = impossible.

Reset vector

the word at 0xFFFE/0xFFFF
Definition
The memory word that holds the address where execution begins after reset. On MSP430 it sits at the top of the vector table (0xFFFE, little-endian, 16-bit even on CPUX) and is data — a pointer placed by the linker as part of the firmware image, not a property of the silicon.
Project example
_reset_vector_pc() reads self._memory.get(0xFFFE) (low byte) and get(0xFFFF) (high byte) and assembles ((hi or 0) << 8) | (lo or 0). probe_cpu_reset_vector_pc writes 0x00/0xC0 and asserts reset lands at 0xC000.
Usage
"Load the image's reset vector with two MEMORY:WRITEs and assert CPU:RESET lands on the entry point — that's the startup-flow test the old constant-PC model couldn't express."
Contrast with: a fixed reset address (AVR/8051/x86 style)
In those families the reset location holds an instruction and the start address is baked into the silicon. On MSP430 (like the 6502 and Cortex-M) the vector holds an address that hardware dereferences — change the firmware image and reset lands somewhere else, no silicon involved.

PUC-time PC fetch

SLAU367P §1.2 — BOR → POR → PUC, then read 0xFFFE
Definition
The final step of every MSP430 reset chain (brown-out reset → power-on reset → power-up clear): hardware performs a memory read of the reset vector and loads that word into the PC. Reset is a fetch, not a jump to a constant — and only the PC is hardware-loaded; the stack pointer is set up by startup code.
Project example
Both _cpu_reset() and the *RST path now run self._pc = self._reset_vector_pc(), replacing the literal self._pc = 0xC000. The default when no vector exists is 0x4000 — the FR5994's FRAM code start — because 0xC000 was, per the audit, "not FR5994-specific".
Usage
"After a wrong WDT password a real part takes a PUC — which means a fresh PC fetch from 0xFFFE, not a teleport to some magic constant."
Contrast with: the simulator's old constant-PC reset
The old model conflated the mechanism (fetch) with a value (0xC000) — and got the value wrong for this part too. A constant encodes "reset behaviour belongs to the chip"; the fetch encodes the truth: it belongs to the loaded firmware. probe_wdt_stub had silently depended on the constant and had to switch to a captured pc_before.

Write masking width

value & 0xFFFFF — the width you mask to IS the model
Definition
The bit-width used when a stored-state model truncates a write to a register's physical size. Masking itself is the faithful policy for data registers (only N flip-flops latch), but the mask constant asserts which hardware is being modelled — masking a CPUX register to 16 bits models a different CPU.
Project example
The entire register half of 07f1f69 is one digit: & 0xFFFF → & 0xFFFFF in _cpu_reg(). Before it, CPU:REGISTER 9,0x28000 stored 0x8000 — a valid-looking address in the wrong 64-KB page, with no error queued.
Usage
"Grep every mask in the device model and ask whose datasheet each width came from — a wrong write-masking width is silent by design."
Contrast with: validation (reject with -222)
Masking accepts and truncates, mirroring flip-flop behaviour; validation refuses states with no hardware existence. The same commit uses both: registers mask to 20 bits, while the PC rejects odd or over-wide values — because an odd PC isn't "a value that got truncated", it's a state that cannot exist.

Binary compatibility

old 16-bit binaries run bit-identically on CPUX
Definition
The guarantee that an existing compiled artifact runs unchanged on a newer CPU. CPUX achieves it with the upper-bits contract (SLAU367P §4.3): 16-bit writes clear register bits 19:16, 16-bit reads can't see them — so legacy code can neither set nor observe the extra width, and only new extended instructions opt in.
Project example
Why the simulator masks to 0xFFFFF instead of validating: any value up to 20 bits is a state some instruction sequence can produce, whether legacy (upper bits zero) or extended (upper bits meaningful). The model must hold both worlds in the same self._registers list — sixteen plain ints, each up to 0xFFFFF.
Usage
"We didn't recompile the bootloader when we moved to the FR5994 — binary compatibility means its 16-bit code runs as-is, blind to the four page bits above it."
Contrast with: source compatibility
Source compatibility means the code recompiles for the new target (possibly to different instructions); binary compatibility means the existing machine code executes identically with no rebuild. CPUX offers the stronger, binary kind — which is exactly why its registers can be wider without any old program noticing.

| word alignment | Words live at even addresses; PC bit 0 is architecturally always 0 (SLAU367P §4.3.1) — an odd PC has no silicon state. `CPU:PC 0x4001` → -222 "PC must be word-aligned"; plain memory stays byte-addressable (`MEMORY:WRITE 0xFFFF,…` is fine). |
| reset vector | The little-endian 16-bit word at 0xFFFE/0xFFFF holding the post-reset entry address — firmware data placed by the linker, not a chip property. `_reset_vector_pc()` assembles `((hi or 0) << 8) \| (lo or 0)`; being 16-bit, reset always lands below 0x10000. |
| PUC-time PC fetch | The end of every BOR→POR→PUC reset chain (SLAU367P §1.2): hardware loads the PC by reading the reset vector. `_cpu_reset` and `*RST` now call `_reset_vector_pc()` (default 0x4000, the FR5994 FRAM code start) instead of the old wrong-part constant 0xC000. |
| write masking width | The bit-width a stored-state model truncates writes to. Masking is the faithful policy for data registers, but the constant asserts which hardware is modelled — 07f1f69's register fix is one digit, `& 0xFFFF` → `& 0xFFFFF`, versus the PC's reject-with--222 policy. |
| binary compatibility | Existing machine code runs unchanged on the newer CPU: on CPUX, 16-bit writes clear register bits 19:16 and 16-bit reads can't observe them, so legacy binaries neither set nor see the extra width — only extended instructions (MOVA/CALLA/.A) opt in. |
